title: Subhash C Kashyap, the Man Who Defined How India's Parliament Works, Is Dead at 97
excerpt: The former Lok Sabha Secretary-General authored over 100 books on constitutional law and served Parliament for nearly four decades, from Nehru's first Lok Sabha to the ninth.
body:
Subhash C Kashyap, one of India's most respected constitutional experts and the former Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha, died at his Sainik Farm residence in New Delhi on Thursday morning. He was 97. The cause was cardio-pulmonary arrest following age-related complications, officials of the Lok Sabha Secretariat said.

His death has drawn tributes from across the political spectrum, a rare consensus in a Parliament whose procedures he spent a lifetime refining.

## A Career That Spanned Independent India

Kashyap served the Indian Parliament for 37 years, from the time of Jawaharlal Nehru's first Lok Sabha through the ninth. He rose through the ranks to become Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha in 1983, a position he held until 1990. During that tenure, he played a pivotal role in standardising parliamentary procedures, codifying precedents, and strengthening the institutional credibility of the lower house.

But his influence extended far beyond the procedural. Kashyap authored more than 100 books and hundreds of research papers on constitutional law, parliamentary practices, political reforms, and grassroots governance. His writings remain authoritative references for legislators, academics, law students, and anyone who has ever tried to understand how India's democracy actually functions at the level of rules and conventions.

Born on May 10, 1929, in Chandpur, Bijnor, in what was then the United Provinces, Kashyap grew up in a family of freedom fighters. He participated in the independence movement as a teenager, leading student protests first in Bijnor and then in Meerut. His higher education took him from Allahabad to New Delhi, Washington DC, London, and Geneva. Before joining Parliament, he worked as a journalist and an assistant professor at Allahabad University, and trained as an advocate at the Allahabad High Court.

## The Constitution's Living Encyclopedia

Kashyap was a member of the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution under the Vajpayee government, where he chaired the drafting and editorial committee. More recently, he was part of the high-level committee headed by former President Ram Nath Kovind tasked with preparing the legal framework for simultaneous elections across India, a proposal that remains one of the most debated constitutional questions in the country.

He also served as the first Indian to head an international organisation, leading the International Centre for Parliamentary Documentation at the Inter-Parliamentary Union in Geneva until 1983. He was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 2015 in recognition of his contributions to public service.

## Tributes Pour In

Prime Minister Narendra Modi described Kashyap as "one of India's foremost constitutional scholars" in a post on X. "His contributions to parliamentary and constitutional discourse enriched our society. His writings and commitment to strengthening democratic institutions were noteworthy," Modi wrote.

President Droupadi Murmu said Kashyap "enriched the study of the Constitution and the development of the parliamentary system with his erudition and insight." Vice President CP Radhakrishnan called him "a living encyclopedia of the Indian Constitution and parliamentary system."

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla described his passing as "a profound loss to Indian parliamentary democracy, constitutional discourse, and public life," adding that Kashyap "left an indelible mark of his scholarship and foresight in every role."

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said Kashyap "made an enduring contribution to India's legal and intellectual landscape" through his "numerous books that illuminated the complexities of the Constitution and parliamentary democracy."

## A Legacy in Rules and Words

For those outside the world of constitutional scholarship, Kashyap's contributions may seem abstract. But every time a Speaker rules on a point of order, every time a committee follows a procedural precedent, every time a debate over the separation of powers references established convention, his work is present. He did not simply observe India's parliamentary system. He built the manual for how it operates.

Kashyap is survived by his wife, two sons, and a daughter. His life's journey, from a teenage freedom fighter in Bijnor to the nation's foremost authority on how its democracy works, leaves behind a body of work that will outlast any single Parliament.
